headline: Hosoi was fososhi, then lost its shi ending and its medial k.
Chikara is a compound of 霊 (chi, “power, life force, essence”) plus 柄 (kara, “source, origin”).
San went */sam/ → /samu/ → /saɴ/, from Middle Chinese 三.
Aka is Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *aka, and the source gives nothing earlier.
Kudasai is the imperative of 下さる (kudasaru, “to give”), the honorific form of 呉れる (kureru).
Inoru is 斎 (i-, prefix expressing sacredness) plus 宣る (noru, “to say or express an intention, usually to a deity”).
Onaji is irregular even in Classical Japanese, mixing -i adjective and -na adjective behavior.
Otoko may be おと (oto, “young?”) plus 子 (ko, “child”), compared with 少女 (otome).
Motsu is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, with cognates across the Ryukyuan languages.
Jisho “dictionary” repurposes an older jisho meaning “letter of resignation”.
Kuni appears in the Kojiki of 712, and is perhaps related to Middle Chinese 郡 (“commandery”).
Hare is the stem of the verb 晴れる (hareru, “to be clear (of weather)”).
Orei is 御 (o-, honorific prefix) plus 礼 (rei, “bow”).
Junbi is ultimately from Middle Chinese 準備, and attested from the early 1800s.
Onēsan is 御 (o-) plus 姉 (nē) plus さん (-san).
Nakunaru is 無い (nai) in -ku form plus なる (naru): literally “to become not, to become nonexistent”.
Amai was amashi in Early Middle Japanese, first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Ban is from Middle Chinese 晚 (MC mjonX).
Kare is 彼 (ka, “that, yon”) plus れ (-re); the male sense of “he” only arose later.
Okonau may be おこ (oko, from 起く) plus なふ (nafu), though the source calls that suffixation unusual.
Shinpai can be analyzed as 心 (shin, “heart”) plus 配 (hai, “to concern oneself with”).
Deru was idu: the initial i fell out in compounds, and du shifted to -deru only later.
Rei is from Middle Chinese 零, whose original meaning was a small rainfall.
Maiasa is 毎 (mai-, “every”) plus 朝, read either あさ (asa) or ちょう (chō).
Hiku “to play (an instrument)” is derived from 引く (hiku, “to pull”).
Te is from Proto-Japonic *tay, and the source invites comparing 目 (me, ma-, “eye”).
Ni is from Middle Chinese 二 (nyijH, “two”).
Tobu is first attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE, from Proto-Japonic *tənpu.
Hen is from Middle Chinese 變 (MC pjenH).
Naru is possibly a verbalization of na-, the bound form of 音 (ne, “sound”).
